passage:
Subject: Thursday's client pitch

Hi Ujjwal,
I wanted to write this instead of saying it in the corridor. This morning you mentioned your migraine is back and that you're "drowning" in the vendor files, so the pitch may be rough. I noticed you said something similar before the March review and before the budget meeting. I'm not saying you aren't tired or unwell; only you know that. I just wonder if these big presentations feel heavier than they need to.
So, for what it's worth: nobody on this team needs the pitch to be perfect. Your slides in March were clear, and the client asked you the follow-up questions, not me. If Thursday is a bit messy, it's still your work, and we'll learn from it together. If you like, we can do a dry run Wednesday at five.
Parveen

qa.q: When had Ujjwal said something similar before?
qa.a: Before the March review and before the budget meeting.

qa.q: What is Parveen thinking about why Ujjwal mentions the migraine and the vendor files?
qa.a: Parveen wonders whether the big presentations feel too heavy, and whether warning that the pitch may be rough gives Ujjwal a cushion in case it isn't perfect.

qa.q: Which part of Parveen's email gives Ujjwal the most useful choice?
qa.a: The offer of a dry run on Wednesday at five lets Ujjwal prepare with support, so full effort feels safer than an early excuse.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading that the pitch doesn't need to be perfect?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel noticed and a little exposed, but also relieved that a messy Thursday won't cost the team's respect 🙂.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate's pre-presentation illness and overload pattern and writes to reassure that effort and imperfection are welcome.

passage: You asked what I've learned as a team lead this year? One thing, about Hrithik. I'm Tejas, by the way, for anyone new listening. Hrithik is sharp, really sharp. But every single time we had a demo for the directors, the day before, he'd come to my desk: "Bro, my back's killing me," or "I've got three deadlines, so this might be half-baked." At first I just said, "Take it easy." By the fourth time I saw the pattern. So before the October demo I took him for chai and said, "Listen, you've never given a bad demo. And if one day it's average, that's fine. I'd rather see you try fully and stumble than hold back." He looked at his cup for ages. The next day, no warning speech. The demo wasn't perfect. It was good.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say the day before demos?
qa.a: "Bro, my back's killing me," or "I've got three deadlines, so this might be half-baked."

qa.q: What does Hrithik's long look at his cup suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the words touched something, perhaps relief or embarrassment that the pattern had been seen and that he didn't need a cushion.

qa.q: What changed when Tejas stopped saying 'Take it easy'?
qa.a: By naming the pattern kindly over chai and saying an average demo was fine, Tejas made full effort feel safe, and Hrithik dropped the warning speech.

qa.q: Why might Hrithik have needed the warning speech in the first place?
qa.a: Presenting to directors may have felt like a test of how sharp he is, so a sore back or three deadlines kept a reason ready if it went badly.

grounding: A team lead describes noticing a teammate's pre-demo excuses and reassuring him that trying fully is welcome even if imperfect.

passage: Anjali here, writing this down because I keep thinking about it. Joseph sits next to me on the hospital admin team. Before the quarterly audit presentation, he told three people he had a fever coming on. Before the one in June, it was "I haven't slept, the rota is killing me." Both times, his presentation was actually fine. I couldn't tell if he was really unwell; he might have been. But on Monday, when he started with "I'm so overloaded, don't expect much," I said, "Joseph, whatever you bring is welcome. You've prepared, and if a slide goes wrong, we'll fix it together." He blinked, laughed a little, and said, "Okay. Okay." On Wednesday he presented without any warnings first. His hands shook a bit at the start. Then they didn't.

qa.q: What did Joseph say before the quarterly audit presentation?
qa.a: He told three people he had a fever coming on.

qa.q: Why might Joseph laugh a little and say 'Okay. Okay.'?
qa.a: He may have felt caught but also relieved; hearing that his effort was welcome loosened his need for a ready excuse.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Instead of only sympathising, Anjali said whatever Joseph brought was welcome and slides could be fixed together, which lowered the stakes.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Joseph without a warning ready?
qa.a: His hands shook at first, showing it took courage to present with no cushion, and then he steadied.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate's pattern of illness and overload before presentations and reassures him that effort is welcome.

passage:
Monday: The quarterly review was on Friday, and Francis had the second slot. At stand-up, Francis mentioned a sore throat 'coming on' and three urgent tickets. Samir remembered the same two things before the last review, and the one before that. He felt a flash of irritation: again?
Wednesday: Samir found Francis at the coffee machine. 'Throat any better?' Francis rubbed the back of the neck. 'Honestly, if the talk's rough, it's because I'm running on empty.' Samir kept his voice light. 'Nobody's expecting a perfect talk, you know. Last time your rough version still had the best numbers. I'd rather see you try it properly and trip a bit.' Francis laughed awkwardly, then went quiet.
Friday: Francis presented without mentioning the throat. One chart was wrong and got fixed live. Afterwards Francis caught Samir's eye and nodded.

qa.q: What two things did Francis mention at Monday's stand-up?
qa.a: A sore throat 'coming on' and three urgent tickets.

qa.q: What did Samir feel on noticing the pattern, and why?
qa.a: Samir felt a flash of irritation, 'again?', because the same excuses had come before the last two reviews as well.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Samir chose to reassure rather than accuse: nobody expects a perfect talk, and a real try is welcome even if it trips; that took the pressure off, so Francis presented without the throat story.

qa.q: What might Francis have been afraid of before each review?
qa.a: Francis may have feared that a weak talk would show a lack of ability; illness or workload made a poor result explainable, until Samir made imperfection feel safe.

passage:
Jasleen, sit a minute. Twice this week you've told me you might be coming down with something before Thursday's board meeting. Let me tell you about Rakesh.
When I was twenty-five, at the insurance office in Chandigarh, Rakesh sat beside me. Clever man. And every time he had to present to the regional head, the day before there'd be a headache, or his mother visiting, or 'I've had no time at all.' I'll admit I resented it a little; I was presenting too, and I had no excuses.
Then one evening I said to him, 'Rakesh, if you try your best and it's ordinary, that's allowed. We'll still sit together at lunch.' He laughed at me: 'Alka, you sound like my mother.' But the next time, no headache. His talk was a bit dull, and he was fine.
So, Jasleen. Try fully. Ordinary is allowed.

qa.q: Where did Alka work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At the insurance office in Chandigarh.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel about Rakesh's excuses, and why?
qa.a: Alka resented them a little, because Alka was presenting too and had no excuses to lean on.

qa.q: What did Alka choose to say to Rakesh, and why did it help?
qa.a: That trying his best and being ordinary was allowed, and they would still sit together at lunch; it made an imperfect result safe, so the excuse was no longer needed.

qa.q: How might Jasleen hear this story, given the week's talk of coming down with something?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel gently caught out on recognising the pattern, but also relieved that an ordinary, honest try at Thursday's meeting would be welcome.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing a colleague's pre-presentation excuses and reassuring him that full effort with an ordinary result was welcome.

passage: The client presentation had been moved up to 10 a.m., the rain had flooded half the roads, and the team was racing. At 8:30 Vasudha messaged the group: 'Bit of a migraine and swamped with the audit, so my section might be rough.' Tenzin read it and felt a flicker of irritation. It was the fourth time. A cold before the board review. 'Crazy week' before the investor call. Always just before, never after. And every time, Vasudha's section turned out fine. Tenzin wondered whether the message was less about the headache and more about having a cushion ready in case the slides weren't perfect. At 9:40, while the others set up, Tenzin sat down next to her. 'Hey. Rough is okay. We want your part, not a perfect part. If something doesn't land, we'll handle it together.' Vasudha looked surprised, then her shoulders dropped. She presented clearly and didn't mention the headache again.

qa.q: When had the client presentation been moved to?
qa.a: It had been moved up to 10 a.m.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel reading Vasudha's message, and why?
qa.a: Tenzin felt a flicker of irritation, noticing it was the fourth warning just before a big presentation, and then wondered whether it was protection against imperfect slides.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's words do for Vasudha?
qa.a: They said imperfect effort was welcome and the team would share any problems, removing her need for an advance excuse.

qa.q: Why might Vasudha send such messages before every big presentation?
qa.a: She may be afraid of being judged if her part isn't perfect, so an early excuse gives her a cushion in case things go wrong.

grounding: On a rushed morning, a colleague notices a teammate's habit of mentioning illness or overload before big presentations and reassures her that imperfect effort is welcome.

passage: In the Pune office, the quarterly pitch to the regional heads was at four. At two, Shreya leaned over the partition. 'Just so you know, I've had a fever since last night, and I've been drowning in tickets, so my numbers slide will be a bit messy.' Nandini nodded, but inside something itched. Before the last pitch it had been a stomach bug. Before the one in March, 'three deadlines at once'. And every time, Shreya's slide had been sharp. Nandini had started to resent these warnings; they made it sound as if the rest of them had it easy. But watching Shreya chew her pen, Nandini saw fear, not laziness. At 3:45 she said quietly, 'Your slide doesn't need to be perfect. You worked on it. That's what we need. If a number's off, we'll fix it after.' Shreya let out a breath. 'Okay,' she said. 'Okay.'

qa.q: What time was the quarterly pitch?
qa.a: The pitch was at four.

qa.q: What did Nandini feel about Shreya's warnings, and how did that change?
qa.a: Nandini had started to feel resentful, as if the rest of them had it easy, but seeing Shreya chew her pen she sensed fear and felt more sympathy.

qa.q: What did Nandini say that helped?
qa.a: That the slide didn't need to be perfect, that the effort was what counted, and that any wrong number could be fixed afterwards.

qa.q: Why might Shreya mention a fever and being overloaded before each pitch?
qa.a: She may be anxious about being judged, so the warning gives a ready explanation if her slide falls short.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate's built-in excuses before each pitch, moves from resentment to understanding, and reassures her that effort is enough.

'Morning,' Maria said, dropping into her chair. 'Warning: my throat's scratchy and I slept four hours, so the demo might be a disaster.'
Harish turned from his screen. 'The demo for the ministry team?'
'That one.'
'Like the sprained wrist before the board review.'
Maria laughed. 'Okay, that was real.'
'I believe you. And "totally swamped" before the client launch?'
'Also real.' She paused. 'Why are you listing these?'
'Because every time, you give the warning, and then you do brilliantly. I started to think maybe the warning is there in case you don't.'
Maria was quiet. 'Maybe.'
'You know what I'd rather hear? "I prepared, let's see."'
'And if it goes badly?'
'Then it went badly after you tried properly, and we learn something. Nobody here needs you to be perfect.'
Maria picked up her notes. 'I prepared,' she said. 'Let's see.'

qa.q: What happened before the board review?
qa.a: Maria had a sprained wrist before the board review.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he listed Maria's warnings?
qa.a: Harish felt curious and a little concerned, suspecting the warnings were a cushion against falling short rather than real predictions.

qa.q: What did Harish offer instead of the built-in excuse?
qa.a: A new phrase, 'I prepared, let's see', and reassurance that a poor result after real effort is fine and something to learn from.

qa.q: How does Maria respond to being noticed?
qa.a: Maria goes quiet, admits it might be true, and then tries Harish's phrase, seeming relieved.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate always announces illness or overload before a big demo and reassures her that effort and imperfect results are welcome.

passage:
I've sat next to Elizabeth for a year, and I only noticed the pattern in March.
Before the quarterly review, she mentioned a migraine. Before the client pitch in June, it was “I'm so overloaded I haven't even looked at the deck properly.” Before the board demo, a sore throat. Every time, she'd say it where the whole team could hear.
I'll admit I was a bit resentful at first. I'd been carrying some of her slides.
Then I watched her before the demo: hands cold, rereading the same line, checking the clock. She wasn't lazy. She was scared, and the excuse was ready before the first slide.
Afterward, I told her quietly, “You were good today. And honestly, you'd be welcome up there with a half-perfect deck. Nobody's waiting for you to be flawless.”
She looked at me for a long moment and said, “Thanks, Mridul.”

qa.q: What did Elizabeth mention before the board demo?
qa.a: She mentioned a sore throat.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel at first about Elizabeth's pattern, and what changed?
qa.a: Mridul felt a bit resentful about carrying her slides, then understood she was scared and felt more sympathetic.

qa.q: What did Mridul say that could help Elizabeth, and why?
qa.a: That she'd be welcome even with a half-perfect deck; it takes away some of the fear that drives her to prepare excuses.

qa.q: What might it be like for Elizabeth to hear this from a colleague?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt surprised and relieved that someone noticed her fear and accepted her without judging her.

grounding: The colleague's reflection shows someone noticing a teammate's built-in excuses before presentations and reassuring her that effort and imperfect results are welcome.

passage:
Team manager's note, marketing, 18 July.
Something I observed this week that I want to remember.
Before Tuesday's campaign review, Sangeeta told the room she'd been up with a fever and “hadn't really prepared.” It's the fourth review in a row with a similar announcement.
Anjali, who sits beside her, noticed it too. I saw her look up, frown slightly, then soften. Later I overheard her in the pantry, not accusing, just saying, “Sangeeta, your ideas in there were really strong. You know, it's okay if a slide's rough. We'd rather hear you properly than not at all.” Sangeeta went quiet and then nodded.
Anjali came to me afterwards and asked, gently, whether our reviews feel too high-stakes for newer people. It's a fair point.
Next step: from next month, reviews will open with “work in progress is welcome,” and I'll check in with Sangeeta one-to-one before the next one.

qa.q: How many reviews in a row has Sangeeta made a similar announcement?
qa.a: It was the fourth review in a row.

qa.q: What might Anjali have felt when she first looked up and frowned?
qa.a: Anjali may have felt a flash of irritation or resentment at the repeated excuse, before softening into concern for Sangeeta.

qa.q: Which of Anjali's actions helped, and why?
qa.a: Her private reassurance that rough slides are okay, and raising with the manager that reviews may feel too high-stakes; both lower the fear behind the excuses.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel after the pantry conversation?
qa.a: Sangeeta might feel relieved and understood, knowing a colleague values her ideas even if her preparation isn't perfect.

grounding: The manager's note shows a colleague noticing a teammate's repeated excuses before reviews and reassuring her that imperfect work is welcome.

passage:
Friday night.
Shankar did it again. Before today's investor walkthrough he said, loudly, “Guys, my back's killing me, I barely slept, don't expect much.” Last month it was a stomach bug. Before that, his laptop “crashed.”
I'll be honest, diary, part of me was irritated. I prepared till midnight too. Nobody gets to hear about my bad sleep.
But during the walkthrough I watched him. He was good. Really good. And every time a question came, his eyes went to the door, as if checking for an exit.
He isn't making excuses because he's lazy. He's making them before anyone can judge him.
After, I found him at the tea machine and said, “That was solid, Shankar. And for what it's worth, even if it had been a mess, I'd still want you presenting.” He laughed awkwardly and said, “Seriously?” I said, “Seriously.”
— Uday

qa.q: What did Shankar say before today's investor walkthrough?
qa.a: He said, “Guys, my back's killing me, I barely slept, don't expect much.”

qa.q: How did Uday feel about Shankar's excuses before the walkthrough?
qa.a: Uday felt irritated and a little resentful, having also prepared till midnight without complaining.

qa.q: Why might Uday's words at the tea machine help Shankar?
qa.a: They tell Shankar he's welcome even if it goes badly, which could reduce the fear behind his pre-emptive excuses.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel hearing “Seriously”?
qa.a: Shankar may feel surprised and relieved, perhaps a little exposed, that a colleague noticed his fear and still values him.

grounding: The diary shows a colleague noticing a teammate's excuses before big presentations and reassuring him that imperfect results are welcome.

passage: At the district cooperative bank in Dharwad, Rajni had worked beside Pradeep for two years. She began to notice a pattern. The day before the monthly audit presentation, Pradeep always had a fever, a family emergency, or "too much pending work". Twice Rajni had presented his section for him, and each time she felt a small flash of resentment. But this month she watched him more closely. On the morning of the presentation, he was at his desk early, pale, re-reading his notes, and when she asked how he was, he said, "Not well. Maybe you should do my part." She pulled up a chair. "Pradeep, I think you're more nervous than sick. Every month it's right before the audit." He stared at his notes. "What if the manager finds a mistake?" "Then he finds it, and you fix it. Nobody expects it to be perfect. We just want you to try." After a long pause, he stood up and picked up his file.

qa.q: How many times had Rajni presented Pradeep's section for him?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as she noticed the pattern?
qa.a: Rajni felt a small flash of resentment at covering for him, but also concern once she watched him more closely.

qa.q: Why did Rajni's reassurance help Pradeep present?
qa.a: She named the nerves gently and said mistakes could be fixed and nobody expected perfection, which made trying feel safe.

qa.q: What was Pradeep worried about on the morning of the presentation?
qa.a: He was afraid the manager would find a mistake in his section.

passage: At the design agency in Tokyo, Yuki noticed that Rafael was always "under the weather" before big client presentations. In spring it was a migraine. In summer, he said he'd been up all night with other deadlines and "couldn't give it his best". Each time, the presentation went okay, and each time he said afterwards, "Imagine if I'd been well." On Thursday, with the biggest pitch of the year the next morning, Rafael sighed at lunch. "I think I'm catching a cold." Yuki put down her chopsticks. "Rafael, can I say something? You always feel unwell before the big ones. I wonder if you're giving yourself a way out in case it's not perfect." He laughed awkwardly. "Maybe." "You don't need one. The team would rather have your full effort and a few mistakes than a perfect excuse." He was quiet for a while. That evening, she saw him rehearsing alone in the meeting room.

qa.q: What did Rafael say before the spring presentation?
qa.a: In spring he said he had a migraine.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she decided to speak up at lunch?
qa.a: Yuki felt concerned and a little impatient with the pattern, but spoke gently because she wanted Rafael to do well.

qa.q: What did Yuki say that made it easier for Rafael to try fully?
qa.a: That the team would rather have his full effort and a few mistakes than a perfect excuse.

qa.q: What might Rafael have been feeling when he said he was catching a cold?
qa.a: Rafael was probably anxious about the big pitch and afraid of an imperfect result, so illness offered a way out.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate always mentions being unwell before big presentations and reassures him that full effort with mistakes is welcome.

passage:
The quarterly review was at eleven, and at nine-thirty Tushar walked into the design studio in Bengaluru with a scarf round his neck. "Throat's gone," he told Vijay. "Also I was up till two on the Mehta files. So, heads up, today might be rough."
Vijay nodded, and then noticed it: the sore throat before the March review, the "crazy week" before the client pitch, the headache before the demo. Every big presentation came with a warning attached.
He didn't say that. He pulled up a chair. "Can I say something? The draft you sent yesterday was strong. If today's a bit rough, nobody will think less of you. We'd much rather see your actual work than a perfect show."
Tushar fiddled with the scarf. "You think it's strong?"
"I do. Walk me through the first three slides?"
At eleven, Tushar presented without mentioning his throat once.

qa.q: What reasons did Tushar give that morning for the day being rough?
qa.a: His throat had gone, and he was up till two on the Mehta files.

qa.q: What did Vijay seem to feel when he noticed the pattern?
qa.a: Vijay seemed concerned rather than irritated; the warnings looked like signs that Tushar was nervous about being judged, so Vijay chose reassurance over calling it out.

qa.q: What made Vijay's response helpful?
qa.a: He didn't accuse Tushar of making excuses; he praised the draft specifically, said a rough result would be welcome, and offered a practice run, which made full effort feel safer.

qa.q: How might Vijay's words have felt to Tushar?
qa.a: Tushar's "You think it's strong?" suggests surprise and relief; hearing his real work valued seemed to make the advance excuses unnecessary.
